claude.sample_unit: wearable-study subjects (301 COVID-19 positive, 2,111 negative) used to test the model

links.outcome: AUROC of hospital model on wearable data with vs without local distribution adjustment
links.effect: Baseline AUROC 0.527; sleep-only 0.644; sleep-only plus unsupervised feature transformation from healthy local wearable data 0.740; 25 healthy subjects' data sufficed.
links.quote: Applying feature transformation on the sleep-only features resulted an additional 15% boosting of performance in terms of AUROC (0.740 versus 0.643, red solid line versus green dashed line in Fig. 5 A).

links.outcome: Performance of hospital-trained model applied directly to wearable population with dataset shift
links.effect: Directly applied hospital model performed at chance: AUROC 0.527 (95% CI 0.498-0.566), AP 0.132; five sources of dataset shift identified.
links.quote: This performance was at chance level (95% confidence interval: [0.498, 0.566] for AUROC, [0.122, 0.153] for AP), suggesting that the hospital model failed to generalize when directly applied to wearable dataset.

links.outcome: Generalization of inpatient predictive model to a new population and context (out-of-hospital wearables)
links.effect: Model applied to new population and setting without correction gave AUROC 0.527, near chance; improved to 0.740 only after both corrections.
links.quote: The model performed at chance level without these two corrections and performed at AUROC of 0.74 when and only when both corrections were used.

unlisted_practices: Restricting wearable features to sleep-period data to remove contextual confounders before applying a pretrained model
Unsupervised percentile-matching monotonic feature transformation to correct covariate shift

links.effect: Direct application to wearable daily features: AUROC = 0.527, AP = 0.132; chance-level AUROC CI [0.498, 0.566].
links.quote: This performance was at chance level (95% confidence interval: [0.498, 0.566] for AUROC, [0.122, 0.153] for AP), suggesting that the hospital model failed to generalize when directly applied to wearable dataset.

links.effect: Observed demographic shift: hospital patients older; 20% female in wearable dataset versus 47% female in hospital dataset.
links.quote: The patients from the hospital dataset were older than the subjects from the wearable dataset (Fig. 2 A), and the wearable dataset had an imbalanced sex ratio than the hospital dataset (Figs. 2 B, 20% female in the wearable dataset versus 47% female in the hospital dataset).

links.effect: Using sleep-only features improved AUROC from 0.527 to 0.644, a 22% AUROC boost.
links.quote: Thus, using sleep-only features resulted a 22% boosting of performance in terms of AUROC, suggesting the importance of controlling for contextual confounders when extracting the likelihood of infection from wearables physiological data.

links.effect: Feature transformation on sleep-only features improved AUROC from 0.643 to 0.740, an additional 15% boost.
links.quote: Applying feature transformation on the sleep-only features resulted an additional 15% boosting of performance in terms of AUROC (0.740 versus 0.643, red solid line versus green dashed line in Fig. 5 A).

unlisted_practices: Restrict wearable physiological prediction features to sleep-only measurements to reduce daytime activity confounding.

links.outcome: model discrimination when directly applied to wearable COVID-19 detection without adaptation
links.effect: Direct application of the inpatient model to wearable daily features yielded an AUROC of 0.527 (95% CI 0.498 to 0.566) and AP of 0.132, performing at chance level.
links.quote: This performance was at chance level (95% confidence interval: [0.498, 0.566] for AUROC, [0.122, 0.153] for AP), suggesting that the hospital model failed to generalize when directly applied to wearable dataset.

unlisted_practices: Unsupervised monotonic feature transformation to align input feature distributions and mitigate dataset shift when transferring models across settings
